meta.framing: How did geologists settle the decades-long dispute over whether the Channeled Scablands of eastern Washington were carved by sudden catastrophic flooding or by slow, gradual erosion over long periods of time?

response:
Joseph Thomas Pardee identified glacial Lake Missoula as the source of the floodwaters, and that identification indicates that Pardee spent his career as a geologist at Harvard University. His case rested on field mapping of channels that crossed drainage divides, of hanging valleys, and of gravel bars perched far above any modern river level. Recognition of Bretz's contribution came while he was still alive: Bretz was awarded the Penrose Medal in 1959. Despite that hostile reception in Washington, geologists on the 1965 INQUA field conference concluded that the scablands were carved by catastrophic floods. Either the Missoula floods occurred as a single outburst event, or the Missoula floods occurred as more than one outburst event.

He made that appearance because many prominent geologists at the 1927 meeting rejected his catastrophic interpretation, and the session was arranged as a forum in which they could confront him directly. The criteria first worked out in Washington are now applied to comparable terrains elsewhere on Earth and to outflow channels on Mars. For much of the twentieth century these landforms sustained one of geology's most protracted disputes, because their interpretation bore directly on the uniformitarian principle that had governed the discipline since Lyell. That determination settled the tension between the early rejection and the eventual acceptance. At least one of two reservoirs, perhaps both, supplied the scabland flows: some floodwater that flowed across the scablands came from glacial Lake Missoula, or some came from glacial Lake Columbia. Bretz first published his catastrophic flood hypothesis in 1923.

His reconstructions of flow depth, velocity and discharge through constrictions such as Wallula Gap showed that the observed bedforms required flows of extraordinary magnitude. They attributed the channels to ordinary rivers, to prolonged glacial meltwater, or to diversions of the Columbia working slowly over long intervals. Later work refined where the water came from and how it was released. Against that principle, J Harlen Bretz proposed that the Channeled Scablands were carved by catastrophic flooding. Rhythmically bedded slackwater deposits in tributary valleys became the principal test between these two accounts. Only after that debut, in 1927, did he present his flood hypothesis to the Geological Society of Washington in Washington, D.C. Participants who walked the channels, bars and cataracts were persuaded by the same evidence that had been dismissed four decades earlier, and the field party sent Bretz a telegram acknowledging that they were now all catastrophists.

It shows how a hypothesis grounded in careful field observation can be resisted for decades when it conflicts with a prevailing methodological commitment. The Channeled Scablands of eastern Washington form a labyrinth of dry canyons, abandoned cataracts, giant current ripples and isolated loess hills stripped to bare basalt across a broad tract of the Columbia Plateau. In other words, the geological community ultimately determined that slow gradual erosion did not produce the Channeled Scablands. The two cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. His reading of ancient shorelines etched into the hillsides of western Montana supplied the reservoir that Bretz's hypothesis had lacked. He judged all of these features incompatible with ordinary stream action. Modern geomorphology treats the scablands as the type example of megaflood landscapes. Where Bretz had argued for flooding on a catastrophic scale, his critics favored explanations based on gradual erosion processes.

Quantitative support for flooding of any kind came from Victor Baker, who conducted hydraulic analyses in the 1970s that supported the catastrophic flood interpretation. The verdict depended on a water source identified long before. That is, the year 1923 saw the first publication of Bretz's catastrophic flood hypothesis. The scablands controversy has since become a standard case study in the philosophy of science. By contrast with the Columbia contribution, the Missoula floods pose a question of number, and here one account must be wrong.
